intro.en: Normal values, memory hooks, syndromes and ward routines that round off the paediatric practical exam.

items.summary: Bedside reference ranges for salts, sugar, kidney, liver, thyroid and blood count tests most often quoted in paediatric viva.

head: Test
Usual range in children
rows: ALT and AST (liver enzymes SGPT and SGOT)

viva.q: Quote normal sodium, potassium and calcium.
What haemoglobin range does the book print?
What total count and platelet ranges are given?
viva.a: Total count 4500-11000 and platelets 1.5-4 lakh per cubic mm.

items.summary: Normal ABG band for pH, carbon dioxide, oxygen, bicarbonate and saturation used to spot acidosis and hypoxia in sick children.

viva.q: Quote the normal pH and bicarbonate band.
What PaCO2 and PaO2 ranges are printed?
What saturation counts as normal?

items.summary: Four hourly urine output bands per kilogram that separate normal flow from polyuria, oliguria and anuria.

viva.q: What hourly output counts as normal?
How do oliguria and anuria differ here?
viva.a: Oliguria is below 1 and anuria below 0.5 ml/kg/hour.

viva.q: What marks polyuria?

items.summary: Haemoglobin floors below which anaemia is declared in young children, older children and adults.

viva.q: Below what level is a 4 year old anaemic?
How does the cutoff change after 6 years?
viva.a: It rises to 12 gm% up to 14 years.

viva.q: What are the adult cutoffs?
viva.a: Below 13 gm% for men and 12 gm% for women.

items.summary: Which mosquito carries what: Aedes brings dengue and chikungunya, Culex brings brain fevers, Anopheles brings malaria.

head: Mosquito
Diseases carried
rows: Dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, Rift Valley fever
West Nile fever, Japanese encephalitis, tularaemia

viva.q: Which diseases travel with Aedes?
viva.a: Dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Rift Valley fever.

viva.q: What does Culex carry?
viva.a: West Nile fever, Japanese encephalitis and tularaemia.

viva.q: Which mosquito spreads malaria?

items.summary: Ordered rescue sequence for a severely malnourished child, from warming and sugar correction through feeding, catch up growth and follow up.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book strings the steps on the line HHIDE CMS follows: two Hs for temperature and sugar, then infection, dehydration, enteric feeding, catch up growth, micronutrients, stimulation, follow up and immunisation.

viva.q: What comes first in severe malnutrition?
viva.a: Warming for hypothermia, then correcting hypoglycaemia.

viva.q: Where do feeding and catch up growth sit?
viva.a: After infection and dehydration are handled, feeding starts, then catch up growth.

viva.q: How does the tens step list end?
viva.a: Sensory stimulation, follow up and immunisation.

title.en: Fever with rash: day of appearance

items.summary: Classic day counting table that dates common eruptive fevers from the first to the seventh day of fever.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book offers the line about a very sick patient taking double tablets to fix the 1 to 7 order in memory.

viva.q: Which rashes appear on day 1 and day 4?
viva.a: Varicella on day 1 and measles on day 4.

viva.q: What appears latest, on day 7?
How do dengue and typhus compare?
viva.a: Typhus shows on day 5, dengue on day 6.

items.summary: Six germs that cross the placenta and infect the unborn child, remembered by the letters STORCH.

blocks.title: Agents
bullets: O is printed without an expansion in the book list.

viva.q: Expand the STORCH letters.
viva.a: Syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV and herpes with HIV.

viva.q: Which two share the H?
Why does this list matter in a newborn?
viva.a: These germs cross the placenta and infect before birth.

unsure: The book prints STORCH beside six infections with no expansion for the letter O; nothing is added for O.

items.summary: Three step ladder of Fallot defects built from the same parts: pulmonary narrowing plus septal holes, growing from three to five parts.

head: Complex (hook)
Parts
rows: Pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH), atrial septal defect (ASD)
Pulmonary stenosis, RVH, ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding of aorta
Tetralogy parts plus ASD or PDA (patent ductus arteriosus)

viva.q: What three parts make the trilogy?
What does the tetralogy add?
viva.a: A VSD with overriding of the aorta instead of the ASD.

viva.q: What turns it into a pentalogy?
viva.a: Adding an ASD or PDA to the tetralogy.

items.summary: Why heavy protein loss swells, clots and infects: the complication cluster of childhood nephrotic syndrome on one hook.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book fixes the cluster with the word NEPHROTIC.

viva.q: Why does a nephrotic child swell?
viva.a: Sodium retention with protein loss into urine.

viva.q: Which clotting and infection risks follow?
viva.a: Thrombotic events, a hypercoagulable state and infections.

viva.q: Is blood pressure high or low?
viva.a: Hypertension is part of the cluster.

items.summary: Five feature cluster of Kawasaki disease fixed by the word CRASH, with artery aneurysm as the dreaded outcome.

blocks.title: Criteria
bullets: H: hand and foot desquamation (peeling skin).

viva.q: Expand the CRASH letters.
viva.a: Conjunctivitis, rash, aneurysm, strawberry tongue and hand foot peeling.

viva.q: Which feature threatens the heart?
What tongue change is seen?

items.summary: Six single gene dominant conditions the book groups together, from brittle bones to Marfan build and Noonan face.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book fixes the list with the word DOMINANT.

viva.q: Which brittle bone disease is dominant?
Which dwarfism is on this list?
Name two more members of the group.

items.summary: Medicines that pass into breast milk and must be withheld from a nursing mother, fixed by the word BREAST.

viva.q: Which antibiotic is barred in nursing mothers?
Which mood and seizure drugs are listed?
Name two more barred agents.

items.summary: Two inherited causes of unconjugated jaundice named together in the book under the hook GUN.

viva.q: Which two syndromes share this list?
What type of bilirubin rises in both?

unsure: The book prints only the two names with the word unconjugated and the hook GUN; no detail on severity or types is given, so the mild versus severe split above is standard teaching awaiting review.

items.summary: Eleven feature checklist for systemic lupus erythematosus strung on the hooks MD SOAP BRAIN.

viva.q: Which rashes count in SLE?
viva.a: Malar rash and discoid lupus with photosensitivity.

viva.q: What serositis sites are listed?
Which blood tests support the diagnosis?

items.summary: Two drug cocktails for Hodgkin lymphoma with each letter expanded: COPP and ABVD.

viva.q: Expand COPP.
Expand ABVD.
What is Oncovin?

items.summary: Five major signs that diagnose acute rheumatic fever, fixed by the word CANCER.

viva.q: Expand the CANCER letters.
viva.a: Carditis, arthritis, nodules, chorea, erythema marginatum.

viva.q: Which criterion moves on its own?
Which criterion is a rash?

title.en: Cyanotic heart disease with right to left shunt

items.summary: Seven blue baby lesions where blood skips the lungs, remembered as five Ts plus pulmonary atresia and Ebstein anomaly.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book fixes the list with 5T PE: five T lesions plus pulmonary atresia and Ebstein anomaly.

viva.q: Name three T lesions that cause cyanosis.
viva.a: Tricuspid atresia, TOF and transposition of the great arteries.

viva.q: Which venous return anomaly is listed?
What do PE stand for in the hook?

items.summary: Eight reasons breast milk wins for infant and mother, from fewer allergies to cancer guard and faster maternal recovery.

blocks.title: Benefits A to H
bullets: Allergic conditions reduced in the infant.
Development of IQ, jaws and mouth.
Fitness: quick return to pre-pregnancy shape for the mother.
Guards against breast, ovary and uterus cancer.

viva.q: How does breastfeeding guard the mother?
viva.a: Less postpartum bleeding and less breast, ovary and uterus cancer.

viva.q: What infant gains does the book list?
viva.a: Best food, fewer allergies and better IQ, jaw and mouth growth.

viva.q: What practical gains follow?
viva.a: Close bonding and an economical feed.

items.summary: Four part syndrome linking Wilms tumour with eye, genital and learning defects, remembered by its own name.

blocks.title: Features
bullets: W: Wilms tumour of the kidney.

viva.q: Expand WAGR.
viva.a: Wilms tumour, aniridia, genital abnormalities, mental retardation.

viva.q: Which tumour warns of this syndrome?

items.summary: Seven birth defect cluster spanning spine to limbs, with the book listing exomphalos among the ventral defects.

viva.q: Expand VACTERL as the book lists it.
viva.a: Vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, TE fistula, exomphalos, renal, limb.

viva.q: Which gut and airway defects pair here?

items.summary: Bedside face, hand and tone clues of Down syndrome strung on the hook DOWNS for the short case.

blocks.title: Features
bullets: Dysplastic ears and dysplastic pelvis seen on X-ray.
Overly large tongue with a high arched palate.
Widely spaced first and second toes.
Short broad hands with a single palmar crease.

viva.q: Which hand and eye signs point to Down syndrome?
viva.a: Single palmar crease with slanting eyes and Brushfield spots.

viva.q: What tone and tongue clues help?
viva.a: Floppy tone with a large tongue and high palate.

viva.q: What X-ray clue is listed?

items.summary: Five red flag features that mark an asthma attack as life threatening, fixed by the word CHEST with a PEFR floor.

blocks.title: Red flags
bullets: T: threatening PEFR under 33 percent of predicted in those above 5 years.

viva.q: Expand the CHEST red flags.
viva.a: Cyanosis or coma, hypotension, exhaustion, silent chest, PEFR under 33 percent.

viva.q: Above what age does the PEFR rule apply?
Why is a silent chest alarming?
viva.a: It means almost no air is moving.

items.summary: Five C causes of lasting diarrhoea in children, from bowel inflammation to milk intolerance.

viva.q: Name the 5Cs of chronic diarrhoea.
viva.a: Crohn, ulcerative colitis, cystic fibrosis, coeliac, cow milk intolerance.

viva.q: Which two are inflammatory bowel diseases?

title.en: Brain tumour warning features: BAN HENS

items.summary: Seven headache plus features that warn of a space occupying brain lesion in a child.

blocks.title: Warning features
bullets: S: squint from sixth nerve palsy.

viva.q: Which eye signs warn of a brain tumour?
viva.a: Blurred vision, nystagmus and sixth nerve squint.

viva.q: Which balance and gut features count?
What hormone clue is listed?

items.summary: Seven three part syndromes that examiners love: kwashiorkor, niacin lack, neonatal tetany, diphtheritic palsy, atopic skin, tuberous sclerosis and zinc lack.

head: Condition
Three features
rows: Marked growth retardation, psychomotor change, oedema
Low calcium fits, carpopedal spasm, laryngeal spasm
Palatal palsy, general palsy, loss of accommodation
Learning disability, seizure disorder, skin lesions (ash leaf spots, shagreen patches, adenoma sebaceum)

viva.q: What three Ds mark niacin deficiency?
What triad defines kwashiorkor here?
viva.a: Growth retardation, psychomotor change and oedema.

viva.q: Which skin marks belong to tuberous sclerosis?
viva.a: Ash leaf spots, shagreen patches and adenoma sebaceum.

items.summary: Five bin colours that sort ward waste correctly: yellow, red, blue, black and white.

head: Bin colour
Waste that goes in
rows: Anatomical waste; blood, dressings, soiled waste, cotton swabs
Infective waste; IV sets, cannula, catheters, urine bags
Medicines; unused and IV drugs, bottles, glass
Municipal waste; food and non-medical waste

viva.q: Where do dressings and swabs go?
Where do needles and blades go?
Which bin takes IV sets and urine bags?

items.summary: Hand washing is listed as a tested practical station, but the book prints the heading with no steps to copy.

blocks.title: What the book gives
blocks.text: The book names hand washing steps as a station without printing any step. Learn the standard ward routine of wetting, soaping all surfaces, scrubbing palm to palm with finger and thumb cleaning, rinsing, drying and turning off the tap with the towel, and confirm the local sequence with your teacher.

viva.q: When must ward hands be washed?
viva.a: Before and after touching any patient and after body fluid exposure.

viva.q: Which hand surfaces are most often missed?
viva.a: Thumbs, fingertips and between the fingers.

unsure: The book prints only the heading 'Hand washing steps' with no steps; the routine above is standard ward practice and needs teacher confirmation.
